notes.b: Teams and performers succeed because they organise themselves and plan ahead, not just because they are fit or skilful. Three linked words describe this: structure, strategy and tactics, and each means something different.
points: Structure is the organised arrangement of players or performers, such as a team formation, positional roles (who plays where), a set-piece arrangement or a relay order. It gives everyone a clear place and job.

Strategy is an overall plan, made before the performance, to achieve a goal. It uses the team's or performer's strengths and the opponent's weaknesses, so the plan is built around what you do well and what the opponent does badly.
Tactics are the specific actions used during the performance to carry out the strategy. In short, strategy is the plan and tactics are the moves that deliver it.

One strategy can be carried out through several tactics. When a tactic fails, the tactic changes while the strategy usually stays the same, because the goal of the plan has not changed, only the way of reaching it.
notes.tip: Do not use strategy and tactics as if they were the same word. Say once that strategy is the overall plan and tactics are the in-game actions, then use each correctly.

notes.b: A formation decides where a team's players stand, and a marking system decides how defenders look after attackers. Together they set the basic shape of a team in attack and in defence.
points: A team formation is a fixed arrangement of players by line, which sets how many defend, how many play in midfield and how many attack. Formations are written as numbers from defence to attack.
4-4-2 in soccer means four defenders, four midfielders and two forwards, a balanced shape with solid cover in every area of the pitch.
4-3-3 in soccer means four defenders, three midfielders and three forwards, with wide attackers stretching the defence so that defenders must cover more ground.
Zonal marking means each defender guards an area of the pitch or court and marks any opponent who enters it. Defenders hold their areas rather than following attackers.
Man-to-man marking means each defender is assigned one opponent to mark wherever that opponent moves, so the defender follows that player around the pitch or court.
The basketball 2-3 zone has two players stationed higher and three lower, covering areas of the court rather than individual players.
notes.tip: When asked for a structure or strategy with an example, state the formation or marking system, then say what it does for the team (for example, wide attackers stretch the defence).

notes.b: A set play is a planned, rehearsed arrangement used at a stoppage or restart, so each player knows their position before play resumes. It is a structure because the players are arranged in advance.
points: Kick-outs in Gaelic football: the goalkeeper restarts play from the goal area while team-mates position themselves to win or receive the ball.
Line-outs in rugby: forwards form two lines and the ball is thrown in straight between them, with a lifted jumper contesting for it.

Short corners in hockey: a planned routine from a set position, in which a short pass is played to a team-mate who shoots or passes into the danger area (the area in front of goal where a score is most likely).
A rehearsed restart can create a scoring chance before the opposing defence has organised itself, which is why teams practise these routines in training.
notes.tip: Name the sport and the restart in your answer (kick-out, line-out or short corner) and say how players are arranged before play restarts.

notes.h: Structures in individual and paired activities
notes.b: Structure is not only for big teams. Relay teams and badminton doubles pairs also arrange their performers in advance so that each person's strengths are used.
points: Relay running order: the coach fixes the order of runners in advance, matching each runner's strengths, such as a fast starter or a runner who changes the baton well at speed, to the legs (sections) of the race.
Lanes and order: the runner in each lane and leg is set before the race, so every changeover (the handing over of the baton) is planned.
Badminton doubles, side-by-side formation in defence: each player covers one half of the court, so the whole court is guarded.
Badminton doubles, front-and-back formation in attack: one player stays near the net while the partner stays back to hit smashes (hard downward shots), so the pair attacks from both areas.
notes.tip: For a mixed relay running order, explain why you put each runner on a leg using their strengths, and say why the order might change, for example because of injury or a change in the opposition.

notes.b: Attacking strategies are plans to create scoring chances. Each one works by using the attackers' strengths or by exploiting a weakness in the defence, usually by creating space.
points: Width and depth: wide players stretch the defence sideways while runners move into the space in front of or behind it, so defenders cover more ground and gaps open.
Overlap run: a team-mate runs outside the player with the ball, creating an extra attacker on that flank (side of the pitch).
Fast break in basketball: after a defensive rebound or turnover (winning the ball), the team pushes the ball up the court before the defence is set, using speed and quick passes.

Pick and roll in basketball: the ball-handler dribbles towards a team-mate who sets a screen (a legal block of a defender), then the screener rolls to the basket, forcing a defender to choose between two players.
Playing to the space behind a high defensive line: passes and runs are timed into the gap behind defenders who have pushed up, exploiting slow pace or poor recovery.
notes.tip: When describing a strategy, always add how it uses a strength or exploits a weakness, for example the fast break works because the defence is not yet set.

notes.b: Defensive strategies are plans to win the ball back or stop the opponents scoring. Like attacking ones, each is chosen because it suits your players or targets a weakness in the opponents.
points: Pressing: the team applies pressure close to the opponents' goal to win the ball high up the pitch or court, exploiting a team that struggles under pressure.
Pressing risk: the space left behind the pressing players must be covered, or the press is easily bypassed with one pass.
Deep, compact block: players defend in a tight shape close to their own goal, denying central space and forcing the opponents to play wide.
Double-teaming: two defenders close down one key player, forcing the ball away from the playmaker and exploiting a team that depends on one player.
Zonal and man-to-man marking are also defensive strategies. Zonal marking guards areas and man-to-man marking guards players.
notes.tip: For pressing, state the risk too (space left behind the press). For double-teaming, say why it works: it exploits a team that relies on one player.

notes.b: In net and wall games such as tennis, badminton and squash, players cannot tackle each other, so strategy is about where and how the ball is hit. The aim is to make the opponent's return weak or leave a gap.
points: Serve-and-volley: after serving, the server moves to the net and volleys the return before it bounces, shortening the rally and exploiting a returner who struggles against a player at the net.
Targeting the backhand: the ball is hit to an opponent's weaker side, so the return is harder to control.
Moving the opponent around the court: shots alternate between corners, the baseline (the back line of the court) and the net, so the opponent covers distance and leaves a gap.
notes.tip: Link each strategy to the weakness it exploits: serve-and-volley beats a weak returner, targeting the backhand beats a weak backhand, and moving the opponent tires them and opens gaps.

notes.b: In running and other individual events, the athlete's strategy is how to spend limited energy over the whole race. Starting too fast or too slow can cost the result.
points: Pacing: the athlete distributes effort over the race so that energy lasts to the finish.
Even pace: a steady speed throughout saves energy for a fast finish and avoids early fatigue (tiredness).
Fast start: an early burst gains position but risks fatigue later in the race, because energy is used up early.
Race tactics: sitting in behind a leading group to save energy, then kicking (sprinting) for the line in the final stage of the race.
notes.tip: When comparing pacing strategies, give the benefit and the risk of each: even pace saves energy, a fast start gains position but risks late fatigue.

notes.h: Compositional elements in dance and gymnastics
notes.b: Compositional elements are the design elements used to build a routine: action, space, dynamics, relationships and choreographic form. They are for dance and gymnastics, while games use structures and strategies.
points: Action: what moves are performed, such as travelling steps, balances, turns, jumps, gestures or gymnastic skills.
Space: levels (high, medium and low), pathways (straight, curved or zigzag lines travelled), direction (forward, sideways or backward) and formations such as a line, circle or diagonal.
Dynamics: how the movement is performed, through speed, force (strong or light) and flow (smooth or sudden).
Relationships with other performers: mirroring (copying as if in a mirror), following, or meeting and parting.
Relationships with props: a prop such as a hoop or ribbon changes the shape of the movement.
Relationships with music: movement is timed on the beat or set against it.
notes.tip: Remember the split: action is what moves, space is where, and dynamics is how. Use this to organise an answer that applies the elements to a sequence.

notes.b: Choreographic form is the overall structure of a piece, and approaches such as contrast, climax and transitions shape how it feels. Choreographers choose these so that a routine holds the audience's interest and flows from start to finish.
points: Choreographic form is the overall structure of the piece; the main forms are motif and development, canon, unison, binary and rondo.
Motif and development: a motif (a short movement idea) is repeated and altered by changing its speed, level, direction or dynamics.
Canon: the same movement phrase is performed by each dancer in turn, starting at different times.
Unison: all performers perform the same movement at the same time.
Binary form: two contrasting sections, A then B.
Rondo: a recurring theme alternates with contrasting sections, in the pattern A B A C A.
Contrast: a slow, sustained section followed by a fast, sudden one, so each section stands out. Climax: energy and complexity build to a peak, usually late in the routine.

Transitions: movements that link sections so the change of pattern looks smooth. Applying the elements to a group sequence: the action is a travelling phrase, the space uses a diagonal formation, the dynamics change from sustained to sudden, and performers mirror each other on the beat.
notes.tip: Give the pattern with the form: binary is A B and rondo is A B A C A. Describe how the routine is built.

notes.h: Evaluating how structures and strategies are used
notes.b: Planning a structure or strategy is only half the job. You then check whether it worked, using methods of analysis, and judge it against clear criteria.
points: Video review: the coach replays the performance to check whether players held their positions and carried out the tactics.
Notational analysis: tallying passes, turnovers and scores from each strategy shows which one worked, because the numbers can be compared.
Checklists: each element of the strategy is checked against key principles, such as whether the team kept its shape in defence.
Observation by a coach or peer: a second observer notices what the player cannot see during play.
Criteria: whether the structure or strategy achieved its aim, whether each role was carried out, and how the opponents responded.
Here these analysis methods are applied to a specific structure or strategy.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate, name a method (for example, notational analysis) and then judge the strategy against all three criteria: aim achieved, roles carried out, and the opponents' response.

notes.b: A plan that suits the start of a performance may not suit the end. Good performers change their structure or strategy when the situation changes, and they can say what they changed and why it works.
points: Reasons to modify: the score and time remaining, changes by the opponent, weather or pitch and court conditions, injury or dismissal (a player sent off), fatigue, or a strategy that is not working.
Change formation: an extra defender is added to the back line when protecting a lead, making the defence more compact.
Switch the marking system, for example from zonal to man-to-man marking when one attacker is dominating the game, so that attacker is followed everywhere.
Change the point of attack: play switches from a blocked centre to a wing where the defence is thinner, so attackers meet less resistance.
Pick and roll becomes pick and pop: when the defender stops the roll to the basket, the screener steps out to a shooting position instead, pulling that defender out to guard the shot.
Smaller space: a routine is adapted by using levels and shorter pathways in place of wide travel, so it still fits the area available.
Different music: phrases are shortened or lengthened so that each motif fits the new tempo and beat count.
notes.tip: If asked how to adapt a plan that is not working, name the change and say why it works, as in pick and roll becoming pick and pop because the defender has stopped the roll.

questions.prompt: Explain two strategies that can help a team succeed in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: badminton doubles. Strategy 1, attacking the weaker player: smashes and drops are directed at the opponent with the weaker defence, so the stronger partner is left to cover a large part of the court. It uses the team's accuracy and exploits an uneven pairing. Strategy 2, length in the rally: high, deep clears to the back of the court force the opponents back, so the front of the court opens for a drop shot. It uses the team's stamina and exploits an opposition that defends the back court poorly.

questions.prompt: Describe a strategy or compositional element suitable for a performance plan and outline how you would adapt it if it were not working.
questions.model: Strategy: moving the opponent around the court in tennis. The player plays a wide shot to one corner, then a short angle shot that pulls the opponent forward, then a shot back to the opposite baseline, so the opponent covers distance and leaves a gap. This suits a player with consistent groundstrokes and good court sense. Adaptation: if the opponent anticipates the pattern and is already moving before the third shot, the player changes the sequence, lobbing over the opponent at the net or varying the order of the shots. The reason is that the opponent has learned the pattern, so the change keeps the same aim of moving them off the court while removing their anticipation.

questions.prompt: Name three compositional elements used in a dance or gymnastics routine and give an example of each.
questions.model: Action: a travelling phrase of skips followed by a balance held on one leg before a turn. Space: a diagonal pathway across the floor, with the performer moving from a high level down to a low level. Dynamics: a sudden burst of speed followed by a sustained, slow movement, which contrasts the two halves of the phrase.
